title: Data collection: primary and secondary data
summary: What data collection is, the two kinds of data (primary and secondary), their examples, their characteristics and the side-by-side comparison table.

chunks.heading: What data collection means
chunks.explanation_md:
This module opens with a simple idea. **Data collection** is the **systematic process of gathering information for research or analysis**.

The word *systematic* matters: you follow a plan, you do not just grab whatever numbers are lying around.

The slide also tells you why the plan matters: **choosing appropriate sources and methods ensures the reliability and relevance of results**. Pick the wrong source or method and your results can be unreliable or beside the point.

chunks.heading: Primary data: first-hand and specific
chunks.explanation_md:
**Primary data** is **first-hand data collected by the investigator specifically for a purpose**. You go out and get it yourself.

**Examples from the slide:** observations, surveys, lab experiments, interviews and physical tests.

**Characteristics of primary data:**
- **Original** and **specific to the research question**.
- **Often more accurate and up-to-date**.
- Involves **higher cost and time investment**.
- The **researcher controls the collection process**.

So primary data fits your question closely, but you pay for it in money and time.

chunks.heading: Secondary data: already out there
chunks.explanation_md:
**Secondary data** is **information already collected and available through other sources**. Someone else did the gathering; you use what exists.

**Examples from the slide:** government reports, academic articles, books, databases and institutional records.

**Characteristics of secondary data:**
- It **already exists**, so it is **typically less expensive and quicker to access**.
- But it **may lack specificity or accuracy for current research**.
- There is **possible bias or outdatedness**.

So secondary data is cheap and fast, but it was not built for your exact question.

chunks.heading: Primary vs secondary: the comparison table
chunks.explanation_md:
The professor puts both side by side. Learn this table as it is:

| Feature | Primary data | Secondary data |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Collected first-hand | Pre-existing data |
| Sources | Surveys, experiments, interviews | Reports, articles, records |
| Advantages | Accurate, relevant | Cost-effective, accessible |
| Drawbacks | Costly, time-consuming | Possible lack of fit, bias |

Notice how the two columns mirror each other: primary is accurate but costly; secondary is cost-effective but may not fit.

questions.stem: Define primary data. Give its examples and two characteristics.
questions.model_answer_md:
Primary data is information the researcher gathers personally for the study at hand.

- **Definition:** first-hand data collected by the investigator **specifically for a purpose**.
- **Examples:** observations, surveys, lab experiments, interviews and physical tests.
- **Characteristics:** it is **original** and **specific to the research question**, often **more accurate and up-to-date**, and the **researcher controls the collection process**.
- **Cost:** it involves a **higher cost and time investment**.

So primary data gives a close fit to the research question, but it costs more to collect.

questions.stem: What is data collection, and why does the choice of sources and methods matter?
questions.model_answer_md:
Data collection is the starting point of any piece of research or analysis.

- **Meaning:** it is the **systematic process of gathering information** for research or analysis.
- **Why choice matters:** choosing **appropriate sources and methods** ensures the **reliability and relevance** of the results.
- **Two broad sources:** data can be **primary** (collected first-hand) or **secondary** (pre-existing).

In short, good results depend on gathering data in a planned way from the right source.

Sources can be primary or secondary

questions.stem: Write a short note on secondary data: meaning, examples and characteristics.
questions.model_answer_md:
Secondary data is information that someone else has already gathered.

- **Meaning:** information **already collected and available through other sources**.
- **Examples:** government reports, academic articles, books, databases and institutional records.
- **Strengths:** it **already exists**, so it is typically **less expensive and quicker to access**.
- **Limits:** it **may lack specificity or accuracy** for the current research, and there is **possible bias or outdatedness**.

Secondary data saves time and money but must be checked for fit before use.

questions.stem: Differentiate between primary data and secondary data on definition, sources, advantages and drawbacks. Which would you choose, and when?
questions.model_answer_md:
Every study must decide whether to collect fresh data or use data that already exists. The two options differ on several features.

| Feature | Primary data | Secondary data |
|---|---|---|
| **Definition** | Collected **first-hand** by the investigator for a specific purpose | **Pre-existing** information already collected and available through other sources |
| **Sources** | Surveys, experiments, interviews (also observations and physical tests) | Reports, articles, records (also books and databases) |
| **Advantages** | **Accurate, relevant**; original, specific to the research question and often more up-to-date | **Cost-effective, accessible**; typically less expensive and quicker to access |
| **Drawbacks** | **Costly, time-consuming** | **Possible lack of fit, bias**; may be outdated |
| **Control** | Researcher **controls the collection process** | Collected by someone else for another purpose |

**When to choose which:**
- Choose **primary data** when the question is specific and accuracy and relevance matter more than cost and time.
- Choose **secondary data** when budget and time are tight and existing government reports, academic articles or institutional records already cover the question, after checking them for bias and age.
- The two can also be combined, since a data collection plan may use a **primary, secondary or mixed** approach.

**Conclusion:** primary data buys fit and accuracy at a higher cost, while secondary data buys speed and economy at the risk of poor fit, so the choice depends on the research question and resources.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to study the food choices of students. Explain how primary and secondary data could each be used for this study, with their sources, benefits and limitations.
questions.model_answer_md:
The slides give food choices as an example of a research question. Such a study can draw on both types of data.

**Using primary data:**
- The researcher could run **surveys**, **interviews** or direct **observations** of what students choose, since these are primary data methods.
- **Benefit:** the data is **original, specific to the research question** and often **more accurate and up-to-date**, and the researcher **controls the collection process**.
- **Limit:** it involves **higher cost and time**.

**Using secondary data:**
- The researcher could use existing **academic articles, books, databases or institutional records** on the topic.
- **Benefit:** it **already exists**, so it is **less expensive and quicker to access**.
- **Limit:** it **may lack specificity or accuracy** for this study and may suffer from **bias or outdatedness**.

**Recommended approach:** the data collection plan allows a **primary, secondary or mixed** approach. A mixed plan could use secondary sources to understand the topic first and then a survey to get first-hand answers from the students.

**Conclusion:** primary data gives the best fit to the question, secondary data saves cost and time, and combining them balances both.
